items.title: GKI makes it extremely hard to maintain the Linux kernel LTS branch for Android. It serves no real purpose and yet requires a massive amount of work to keep it going. It's adding months of delays to the stock Pixel OS kernel updates and doesn't help any Android OEM in practice.
items.content: GKI makes it extremely hard to maintain the Linux kernel LTS branch for Android. It serves no real purpose and yet requires a massive amount of work to keep it going. It's adding months of delays to the stock Pixel OS kernel updates and doesn't help any Android OEM in practice.

items.title: Google wasted an enormous amount of resources to develop GKI. It was supposed to make it much easier to keep Android devices on an up-to-date kernel. It's a disastrous failure. It does not make it substantially easier because updating kernel drivers for LTS ABI changes is easy.
items.content: Google wasted an enormous amount of resources to develop GKI. It was supposed to make it much easier to keep Android devices on an up-to-date kernel. It's a disastrous failure. It does not make it substantially easier because updating kernel drivers for LTS ABI changes is easy.

items.title: All of the kernel drivers for any devices we'll support are open source. It would be an egregious violation of the GPL to ship driver code specific to Linux without providing all the source code. The drivers are updated alongside the kernel so there's no actual use case for GKI.
items.content: All of the kernel drivers for any devices we'll support are open source. It would be an egregious violation of the GPL to ship driver code specific to Linux without providing all the source code. The drivers are updated alongside the kernel so there's no actual use case for GKI.

items.title: The main purpose of the Android GKI branch is to implement a stable ABI for kernel drivers. The ABI is only stable within an LTS branch. It has no practical use case and a massive maintainability cost. This system collapsed under the massive increase in Linux kernel patches.
items.content: The main purpose of the Android GKI branch is to implement a stable ABI for kernel drivers. The ABI is only stable within an LTS branch. It has no practical use case and a massive maintainability cost. This system collapsed under the massive increase in Linux kernel patches.

items.title: The upstream Linux kernel LTS branches backport a enormous amount of bug fixes including a massive number of security fixes. Android backports much more because they want to ship many of the performance improvements, new features and additional fixes with older LTS branches.
items.content: The upstream Linux kernel LTS branches backport a enormous amount of bug fixes including a massive number of security fixes. Android backports much more because they want to ship many of the performance improvements, new features and additional fixes with older LTS branches.

items.title: The changes required to move the Pixel drivers from 6.1, 6.6 and 6.12 to 6.18 are tiny. The changes needed to use the upstream 6.18 LTS ABI instead of the stable 6.18 GKI LTS ABI are larger but quite manageable. It's preserving all the extra improvements which is extremely hard.
items.content: The changes required to move the Pixel drivers from 6.1, 6.6 and 6.12 to 6.18 are tiny. The changes needed to use the upstream 6.18 LTS ABI instead of the stable 6.18 GKI LTS ABI are larger but quite manageable. It's preserving all the extra improvements which is extremely hard.

items.title: Porting from the 6.1, 6.6 and 6.12 GKI LTS branches to the 6.18 GKI LTS branch is relatively simple and doesn't require a large number of changes.
items.content:
Porting from the 6.1, 6.6 and 6.12 GKI LTS branches to the 6.18 GKI LTS branch is relatively simple and doesn't require a large number of changes.

Porting from GKI LTS to the upstream LTS branch is much harder. Android has thousands of extra backported fixes and improvements.

items.title: Moved our git web server from cgit to stagit to reduce load on the server caused by crawlers, as it only uses static files.
items.content:
Moved our git web server from cgit to stagit to reduce load on the server caused by crawlers, as it only uses static files.

Roughly 99.9% of requests are bots fetching commits and files over and over again at a rate of 50 req/s despite our robots.txt excluding any crawler. Stagit only exposes a small number of files and commits so they are not reachable to bots.

Sadly, many anti-bot protections rely on JS or fingerprinting which come with their own set of problems.

items.title: The most annoying ambiguity I can remember of that kind was the time I wanted to garbage-collect a PDF file: I had hand-edited it to remove a reference to one object in the file from another, and I wanted to make a smaller PDF with the now-unreferenced object completely removed.
items.content:
The most annoying ambiguity I can remember of that kind was the time I wanted to garbage-collect a PDF file: I had hand-edited it to remove a reference to one object in the file from another, and I wanted to make a smaller PDF with the now-unreferenced object completely removed.

If you search for "pdf garbage collection", you feel very foolish, because _all_ the hits are academic articles about garbage collection in general, published as PDFs.

(The answer to that one turns out to be "mutool clean".)

items.title: Got lucky with a web search just now.
items.content:
Got lucky with a web search just now.

I wanted to debug a crash in LLVM. For other programs I'd start by compiling with Address Sanitizer. LLVM's build process is tricky enough that you might not do that the obvious way, so I websearched "build llvm with address sanitizer".

Foolish me! That can also be interpreted as "build an LLVM toolchain that includes ASan for end users to use on the programs they build with it". Most of the hits were about that, and not about the thing I wanted.

But lucky me! I found a Stack Overflow post that recognised the ambiguity and answered _both_ questions. Top marks, that poster.

(The answer is "-DLLVM_USE_SANITIZER=Address".)

I was mostly curious to see whether my code could generate a finite-state transducer for Chair44, able to calculate the combinatorial address of a tile's neighbour given the address of the tile itself, each in the form of a sequence of symbols indicating which slot the tile occupies in its supertile, and that in its supertile in turn, etc.
items.content:
I was mostly curious to see whether my code could generate a finite-state transducer for Chair44, able to calculate the combinatorial address of a tile's neighbour given the address of the tile itself, each in the form of a sequence of symbols indicating which slot the tile occupies in its supertile, and that in its supertile in turn, etc.

But having done that, I don't have a good way to show a pretty picture of it as I do in that blog post, showing the types of all the tiles! Plotting 2D tilings as an SVG is easy, but rendering things in 3D requires getting to grips with a pile of graphics software that I don't normally have occasion to use.

Also, I think it wouldn't look that interesting, because the key point about Chair44 compared to the 'basic' 3D chair tiling is that the sub-chairs are rotated into carefully chosen orientations to make the edge markings match up. But it turns out that the system of three tile subtypes is insensitive to that, because the six sub-chairs that aren't the inner or outer corner are always all the same type. So a colouring of a tiling of space wouldn't show up anything about the interesting properties that turn chairs into Chair44s.

But at least the combinatorial code _worked_, so I know that I can handle more interesting 3D tilings should one show up!

items.title: This is fixable in principle, by extending the specification so that every time it shows two tiles meeting at an 'edge' (or a face), it also specifies some kind of transformation saying how one tile's edge is transformed relative to the other. That transformation is translated into a permutation of the sub-edges, removing the ambiguity.
items.content:
This is fixable in principle, by extending the specification so that every time it shows two tiles meeting at an 'edge' (or a face), it also specifies some kind of transformation saying how one tile's edge is transformed relative to the other. That transformation is translated into a permutation of the sub-edges, removing the ambiguity.

I haven't made that change in full generality. But for the case of Chair44, I was able to bodge it, because each of the 24 facelets of a Chair44 tile has an arrow on it, and the arrow heads must always meet. So I simply hacked on the code to say that sub-edges are numbered 0,1,2,3, and instead of negating them as integers, we negate them mod 4, mapping 1 ↔ 3 and leaving 0,2 fixed. Then we just number the sub-edges so that 0 and 2 are the head and tail of the arrow, and 1 and 3 are the other two corners of the square.

With that hack in the code, my software can run all its combinatorial algorithms on the Chair44 tiling. But now it's _only_ useful for that one 3D tiling, not any more general ones – and the hacked code won't work on 2D tilings any more either! Back on the main git branch, we're still restricted to 2D.

items.title: When two tiles A,B meet at a whole edge, and then both tiles are subdivided into smaller tiles, we need to know which sub-edge of A's edge corresponds to which sub-edge of B's. Otherwise we can't find out which sub-tile of A meets which sub-tile of B.
items.content:
When two tiles A,B meet at a whole edge, and then both tiles are subdivided into smaller tiles, we need to know which sub-edge of A's edge corresponds to which sub-edge of B's. Otherwise we can't find out which sub-tile of A meets which sub-tile of B.

In the plane, there's only one way for two tile edges to meet: they are rotated 180°, so that the sub-edges occur along the edge in some total order, and meet the other tile's sub-edges in the reverse of that order.

My code models this by numbering the sub-edges as integers, symmetric around zero (e.g. −2,0,+2 or −3,−1,+1,+3). Then, sub-edge n of one tile always meets sub-edge −n of the other.

But that doesn't work in 3D, because two polyhedra meet at a face, and if that face has any symmetry at all, then there's _more than one_ way that the sub-faces of that face could match up, depending on how one polyhedron is rotated relative to the other!

So, despite my efforts to make my system purely combinatorial, I had accidentally built in a dependency on 2D, simply in not providing any alternative to the "negate the sub-edge index" policy.

items.title: The substitution system divides a tile into smaller sub-tiles, which also means each 'edge' is divided into 'sub-edges', corresponding to the 'edges' of the smaller tiles.
items.content:
The substitution system divides a tile into smaller sub-tiles, which also means each 'edge' is divided into 'sub-edges', corresponding to the 'edges' of the smaller tiles.

The map describing the subdivision of a single large tile into small ones must state which 'edges' of pairs of small tiles meet internally, and which 'edges' of small tiles correspond to which 'sub-edges' of the exterior of the large tile.

items.title: My code describes a tile as having 'edges': parts of the tile's boundary where it can meet other tiles. They're called edges because normally they're edges of a polygon. Here, they're really faces of a polyhedron, but that _shouldn't_ make a difference.
items.content:
My code describes a tile as having 'edges': parts of the tile's boundary where it can meet other tiles. They're called edges because normally they're edges of a polygon. Here, they're really faces of a polyhedron, but that _shouldn't_ make a difference.

Or _parts_ of faces, because it's simplest to consider Chair44 as having 24 small square faces, most of them coplanar with some of their neighbours to create the larger 'true' faces of the polyhedron.

(The numbering in this diagram is completely arbitrary, and different from what I have in my code, which is also completely arbitrary. If I wanted to publish this properly I'd make up a more sensible numbering system.)

items.title: So, there's been a 3D aperiodic monotile discovered. I have software for handling aperiodic tilings computationally, but only tested so far in 2D. Can it cope?
items.content:
So, there's been a 3D aperiodic monotile discovered. I have software for handling aperiodic tilings computationally, but only tested so far in 2D. Can it cope?

My system works in a purely combinatorial manner, not relying on the geometry of the tiling: it only depends on what tiles exist, which are adjacent via what part of their boundary, and which ones are subtiles of which in the hierarchy of substitutions. So it _ought_ to handle 3D tilings as easily as 2D.

This seemed like a good moment to test that claim! Can I write down, or generate, a combinatorial description of the Chair44 substitution system which my code can handle?

I gave this a try, and found that the answer was yes, _eventually_. But I had missed something subtle, and had to fix it, or rather, bodge it.

items.content:
It would _almost_ work to turn '-n' into an option that says: first sort by length, and then sort lexicographically within strings of the same length. That would correctly sort non-negative integers in any number base at all without needing to be told which base, as long as the digits are represented by characters whose ASCII ordering matches their semantic ordering. It would even correctly ignore 0x prefixes on hex numbers, if there were any.

Not quite, though. That policy wouldn't handle negative numbers, so you'd still have to make a special case for a leading minus sign. And if you were sorting non-integers, then you'd have to spot a decimal point, separate that and everything after it, and use that as a tertiary sort criterion. Ugh.

items.title: You can implement this procedure by only a small change to the obvious technique. Choose a starting exponent in the way I suggested; then choose a random mantissa, but invent one _more_ bit than you needed; finally, use that extra bit to decide whether to round up or down. In a small number of cases, you'll round up to the next exponent, implementing the low end of the catchment area of the next higher power of 2.
items.content:
You can implement this procedure by only a small change to the obvious technique. Choose a starting exponent in the way I suggested; then choose a random mantissa, but invent one _more_ bit than you needed; finally, use that extra bit to decide whether to round up or down. In a small number of cases, you'll round up to the next exponent, implementing the low end of the catchment area of the next higher power of 2.

For once, you don't have to worry about the round-to-even tie breaking rule, because with a real random variable, ties occur with probability zero!

(The simple rule I originally suggested is correct if you're rounding _down_. It's the default option of rounding to nearest that makes things harder.)

items.title: What's the right way to generate a floating-point number representing a sample of a uniformly random variable in the range [0,1]?
items.content:
What's the right way to generate a floating-point number representing a sample of a uniformly random variable in the range [0,1]?

You might think: choose the exponent to be 2⁻¹ with probability 1/2, 2⁻² with probability 1/4, etc (with some fudge when the range runs out). And then, once you've chosen an exponent, choose uniformly at random from the mantissas.

The # ethos is to calculate the mathematically perfect result, and then round that to the nearest representable number. So you must choose each floating-point number x with probability in proportion to its rounding 'catchment area': the range of real numbers above and below x that will round to x.

Well, isn't that what I just said?

No, it isn't – because powers of 2, at the boundary between two exponents, have a catchment area half as big on the left as on the right. So you must choose _most_ numbers with probability 2⁻ⁿ where n varies with the exponent, except that powers of 2 are chosen with probability 2⁻ⁿ + 2⁻ⁿ⁺¹. Arrgh!

#TIL[1] that in #SageMath[2] you can accidentally write a comparison expression that doesn't do a comparison. (Reposted after the previous version was subtly wrong)
items.content:
# that in # you can accidentally write a comparison expression that doesn't do a comparison. (Reposted after the previous version was subtly wrong)

x = QQbar(UniversalCyclotomicField().gen(3))if x == (-1 + sqrt(3)*i) / 2:if x != (-1 + sqrt(3)*i) / 2:

The canonical primitive cube root of unity really is (−1+i√3)/2. So we expect "All is well" and not "Disaster". But in fact we get both:

$ sage z.sageAll is well

Turns out this is because when you compare a QQbar value with some more general algebraic expression, it doesn't do a comparison. It constructs a symbolic expression object that just represents the _notion_ of equality or inequality:

sage: print(x != (-1 + sqrt(3)*i) / 2)(-0.500000000000000? + 0.866025403784439?*I) != 1/2*I*sqrt(3) - 1/2

And those expression objects can evaluate true in a boolean context, simply because they aren't None or False. But they don't _always_. The == comparison seems to work OK, but the != evaluates true unconditionally. #

(The workaround is to coerce the RHS of the expression to QQbar too: 'if x != QQbar(...)'. Then you're comparing elements of the same field and Sage is happy.)

items.title: Replacing the old battery on rechargeable bike lights
items.author: Julia Evans
items.content:
Hello! Recently I needed bike lights for my bike. And I remembered that I already had rechargeable bike lights that I bought ten years ago, that I hadn’t tried in a long time. I tried to recharge them, but after fully charging them, they only worked for maybe 5 minutes before they turned off again.

I don’t know much about electronics, but I’ve been curious about whether it’s possible to fix old electronics for a long time, and this seemed like the perfect repair project because I might just need to replace the battery.

So I went to the local queer makerspace where I’m a member to use the soldering iron and try to do it! I don’t know much about electronics and this post does not contain any safety advice because I don’t know much about safety. I think it’s nice to do projects in a community space where you can get help.

The bike light felt like it was made of silicone, so I cut open the silicone in a haphazard way along something that vaguely looked like a seam.

I definitely ripped some silicone in the process and it was pretty messy but I got it open and found the circuit board.

I don’t know the model number of the bike lights but there’s a photo of them at the end of the post.

step 2: remove the screws

There were some screws attaching things together so I removed them so I could get the circuit board out.

Mostly I tried to remove as few screws as possible because I was worried about losing them or not being able to put them back after. I probably put the screws in a bag or something.

step 3: get the circuit board out

I took out the circuit board. Here’s what it looked like:

You can see where the battery is attached, I think it’s left of RI3 and above Q2.

Here’s what the battery looked like:

step 4: desolder the battery

Here were the steps I ended up following based on the guide & the advice I got:

  1. Use a desoldering pump to remove most of the solder
  2. Once most of it is gone, kind of pull them apart to try to separate them
  3. Also try to avoid getting the battery too hot in the process by taking breaks to let it cool down. I’m not very good with a soldering iron so it took a while.
  4. The battery has an attachment that is welded to the top. For a while I thought I needed to remove this and it seemed impossible, but it turned out the replacement battery comes with that part so actually I was supposed to leave it alone.

step 5: identify the battery

In the picture of the battery in Step 3, you can see it says something like “3” and “LI???77”. There’s a piece of metal that I think is welded or something to the top of the battery. It seemed impossible and also maybe not smart to try to remove so I wasn’t sure how to find out what an “LI????77” was or how to order another one.

I’ve been trying to avoid using LLMs (though I will not get into that because I am exhausted by LLM discourse and I’m sure you are too), but I really had no idea how to figure out what the battery was so I asked an LLM. It gave the response “LIR2477”, which (when I looked it up) looked exactly the same as my battery so I figured that was plausible.

I would be interested to learn non-LLM ways to figure this out though. There must be a way. Lauria showed me how to use DigiKey’s search which was very cool though DigiKey didn’t have that part.

(edit: someone in the replies told me that this kind of coin cell battery is named according to its dimensions, and you can use plastic calipers to measure the dimensions of the battery. So I guess a non-LLM way would be to measure the battery with calipers and try to match it to something on the List of battery sizes Wikipedia page, though that page only mentions CR 2477 and not LIR 2477. It’s a good example of what’s fun for me about trying to avoid LLMs, this “List of battery sizes” page is super interesting and if I use an LLM I might never find it)

I went to AliExpress and ordered:

  1. 2 batteries (I had 2 bike lights and I wanted to fix them both)
  2. some silicone glue to glue things back together

I think the batteries were $3 each and the glue was $8.

step 7: solder the new batteries in and glue it back together

The parts took maybe 2 weeks to arive, and once they arrived, I went back to the makerspace and:

  • soldered in the new batteries
  • put the screws back in. The screws were very small and hard to hold, so at this point I dropped some screws on the ground and couldn’t find them because they were too small. So I just used fewer screws and hoped for the best.
  • used the glue to try to put everything back together.
  • Make a somewhat halfhearted attempt to clamp the parts I was gluing together

Then after waiting some amount of time for the glue to dry I took it home and waited 24 hours for the glue to cure.

Also I took the old batteries to somewhere nearby that accepts old batteries.

The lights work! I have used them to bike at night! I still haven’t needed to recharge them (and tragically I had to order a new Mini USB cable because I got rid of all my Mini USB cables, so I’m still waiting for that), so I still don’t know for sure how long the lifetime of the new battery will be.

Here’s what the light looks like after re-gluing. You can see that I didn’t glue very carefully. It didn’t really go back together that well but I’m hoping it’ll be good enough.

I thought it was really cool that I was able to do this with extremely minimal electronics skills! It cost about $20 CAD to buy the parts, and (whether or not the repair holds up, I’ll try to update this post in the future!), it was fun to try to repair something and learn something new.
